items.title: Nobody called it the Wars of the Roses at the time
items.claim: The wars between Lancaster and York (1455-1487) are remembered for the red and white rose badges. What is the actual history of those symbols?

options.text: Both sides wore rose badges throughout the conflict
The white rose was a Yorkist badge, but the red Lancastrian rose was largely a Tudor-era invention — Henry VII used the union of the roses as propaganda
The roses came from heraldic tradition dating to the Conquest
The name was coined in 1485 by Henry VII himself

items.reveal_title: The Tudor rose was the spin
items.reveal:
Edward IV used a white rose among other badges. The red rose was a minor Lancastrian badge under Henry IV but rarely used during the wars themselves. The 'Tudor rose' (red and white combined) was created after Henry VII married Elizabeth of York in 1486 — the union as legitimising symbol.

The name 'Wars of the Roses' was popularised by Walter Scott's novel 'Anne of Geierstein' (1829). Shakespeare's 'Henry VI Part 1' invented the Temple Garden scene where nobles pluck the rival roses.
items.why: Historical memory is shaped by later spin. The Tudor regime had every reason to dramatise dynastic union; Shakespeare amplified the imagery; Scott named it. Almost none of that was visible in 1460.

items.title: Caesar's assassins included his own protégés
items.claim: Who killed Julius Caesar on 15 March 44 BCE?

options.text: A conspiracy of around 60 senators, led by Marcus Junius Brutus (who Caesar had pardoned and promoted) and Gaius Cassius Longinus, stabbed him 23 times in Pompey's Theatre
Mark Antony alone, in a private quarrel
He died of natural causes; the assassination is a later invention

items.reveal:
Caesar had crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE, defeated Pompey at Pharsalus (48), and been declared dictator perpetuo in February 44 BCE. The conspirators feared a return to monarchy.

The assassination took place at a Senate meeting at the Curia of Pompey. Suetonius and Plutarch describe the scene; the famous 'Et tu, Brute?' is Shakespeare's. Plutarch records Caesar saying 'kai su, teknon?' ('you too, child?') in Greek to Brutus.

The Liberators expected to restore the Republic. Instead they triggered the Liberators' civil war, ending at Philippi (42 BCE) with Brutus's suicide. Octavian became Augustus, first emperor, in 27 BCE — the Republic was over.
items.why: Assassinations rarely produce the political outcome the assassins want. The Liberators killed to save the Republic and accelerated its end — a paradox of political violence visible across history.

items.title: The Western Roman Empire 'fell' in 476 CE with little fanfare

options.text: Rome was sacked and destroyed in a single battle

The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus (a boy of about 16), and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople — contemporaries barely noticed; the date was made significant by later historians
The Senate voted to dissolve the empire

items.reveal:
The Western Empire had been declining for over a century — barbarian federate settlements, Visigothic sack of Rome (410 under Alaric), Vandal sack (455), shrinking tax base, military commanders of barbarian origin holding real power. Romulus Augustulus, installed by his general father Orestes in October 475, was deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476.

Odoacer ruled as king of Italy under nominal Byzantine sovereignty. The Eastern Empire continued until 1453. Edward Gibbon's 'Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire' (1776-89) made 476 the canonical end date.

Modern historians (Peter Heather, Bryan Ward-Perkins, Walter Goffart) debate whether 476 marks 'fall', 'transformation' or simply 'continued change'.
items.why: 'The fall of Rome' is a label imposed centuries later on a gradual process. The boundary between antiquity and the Middle Ages is a periodisation choice — useful for teaching, misleading if treated as a single event.
